[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Sentence and Document Embeddings (Doc2Vec, SBERT) Tutorial"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"In Natural Language Processing, moving from token-level representations to sentence and document-level embeddings is crucial for tasks like semantic search, document clustering, and question answering. This tutorial explores Doc2Vec for unsupervised document representations and Sentence-BERT (SBERT) for dense, context-aware sentence embeddings."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Understanding Doc2Vec"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Doc2Vec (Paragraph Vector) is an unsupervised framework that extends Word2Vec to learn continuous distributed vector representations for pieces of text, ranging from sentences to large documents. It introduces a paragraph token that acts as a memory to remember what is missing from the current context."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Distributed Memory (PV-DM): Acts similarly to Word2Vec CBOW, predicting the next word given context words and a paragraph ID."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Distributed Bag of Words (PV-DBOW): Acts similarly to Word2Vec Skip-gram, predicting words sampled from the paragraph given only the paragraph ID."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"from gensim.models.doc2vec import Doc2Vec, TaggedDocument

data = [["hello", "world"], ["machine", "learning", "is", "fun"]]
tagged_data = [TaggedDocument(d, [i]) for i, d in enumerate(data)]

model = Doc2Vec(tagged_data, vector_size=100, window=2, min_count=1, epochs=40)
vector = model.infer_vector(["hello", "machine"])
print(vector)"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Limitations of Traditional Embeddings and the SBERT Solution"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"While models like BERT provide rich contextual word embeddings, computing semantic similarity between sentences using standard BERT required passing sentence pairs through a cross-encoder, which is computationally expensive for large-scale retrieval (scaling quadratically with the number of sentences)."},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Sentence-BERT (SBERT) modifies the BERT architecture using siamese and triplet networks to derive semantically meaningful sentence embeddings that can be compared using cosine similarity."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Implementing SBERT with Python"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"The sentence-transformers library provides an easy-to-use interface for generating state-of-the-art sentence and document embeddings."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')

sentences = [
    "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.",
    "A fast, dark-colored fox leaps across the sleeping hound.",
    "Natural language processing involves machine learning algorithms."
]
\embeddings = model.encode(sentences, convert_to_tensor=True)

cosine_scores = util.cos_sim(embeddings[0], embeddings[1])
print("Semantic similarity score:", cosine_scores.item())"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Conclusion and Best Practices"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Use Doc2Vec when working with unlabelled text corpora where domain-specific document vectors are needed without heavy pre-trained models. Use SBERT for tasks requiring high semantic accuracy such as semantic textual similarity, semantic search, and clustering."}]
